Hey, it's Evan at OpenAI. I spent my whole career in news, and now I'm here to help journalists use AI to work smarter and faster. Okay, so we have a whole other video on skills. Skills are great. They are reusable instructions like the newsroom recipe. The thing that says, "When I give you this kind of input, I want this kind of output in exactly the same format with the exact same guardrails." But there's another piece to this, agents. Let's talk about the difference first. A skill is essentially a tool in a toolbox. An agent is the AI worker that can put that skill to use. For example, a skill says, "Here's how we make a brief." But the agent says, "Great. Now I will go out, find the material, use the approved tools, follow the workflow, and make that brief to the exact specifications." Just like a person uses their skills to perform a task, an agent does the same thing. So let's try out an example. Imagine you're a reporter covering education for Miami-Dade County Public Schools in Florida. Every week, you need to know what the school board's doing, new agenda items, meeting minutes, budget reports, all that good stuff. Anything that might affect students, teachers, families, transportation, or taxpayer money. So what might that process look like now? You go find the latest public minutes and reports. You open up all the relevant documents. You pull out what's changed. You separate facts from possible story angles. You flag what needs a call, and you format it the same way every time. That's exactly where a skill and an agent work together. The skill is your briefing template. It says, "Always give me the top items, the source document, the date, why it matters, who's affected, money involved, questions to ask," and a section called Needs Human Check. The agent is the workflow that can then go look for the latest material, use your connected tools that your workspace approves, and then apply that skill. So I create an agent called Miami-Dade Education Watch. Its job is to build the reporting brief. Here's the prompt. "Create an agent called Miami-Dade Education Watch. Its job is to help an education reporter monitor Miami-Dade County public school materials. On request, it should search for the latest public school board agendas, meeting minutes, budget reports, audit reports, procurement items, policy updates, and public district reports. It should identify the source, date, and link each item it uses. It should not treat a possible story angle as confirmed fact. When it has the materials, it should use the briefing template skill to return a consistent reporter brief, top items, why each matters, affected students or communities, money involved, documents to open next, questions to ask officials, missing information, and needs human check. Do not publish, email, post, or contact anyone without explicit approval." Okay, now look at what we've built. The agent has a beat, Miami-Dade education. It has a job, find the latest public materials and turn them into a reporting brief. It has limits. It must cite what is used. It cannot turn an angle into a fact. It cannot take action without permission. And it has a skill. The briefing template skill is the newsroom standard for the output. So you're not hoping the agent invents a new format every time. You are telling it, "Use the newsroom template." And here's what you get out. The brief structured exactly as the template requires. The agent should say where it looked. It should show the dates. It should distinguish the board voted from the agenda suggests. It should tell you when it could not access something. It should point you back to a document, not away from it. This is how AI helps without taking over the judgment. It gives the reporter a cleaner starting point. Maybe the brief says there's a new transportation contract. Maybe it flags a facilities report about school air conditioning. Maybe it notices a budget amendment, a tutoring program update, or a disciplinary policy change. This is a map of where to start reporting. Here's really the simplest way to remember the difference. If the work is repeatable, make it a skill. If the work needs to go find things, use tools, follow steps, and come back with an output, make an agent. If the work needs both, let the agent use the skill. And that's really the newsroom sweet spot. The agent does the legwork, the skill keeps the format consistent, and the journalist keeps the judgment. Follow OpenAI Academy for more tips.
